summary: This document specifies conventions for using NIST's post-quantum signature algorithm ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. It also covers how signatures and key material are encoded.

eli5.summary: A signature that even a future quantum computer cannot forge is useful. This tells certificates how to use one such new signature type.

questions: how big is an ml-dsa public key
what is the ml-dsa private key seed format
subtitle: How to put NIST's quantum-resistant ML-DSA signatures and keys into X.509 certificates and CRLs.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates and CRLs need a defined way to carry signatures, public keys and private keys of the new post-quantum signature algorithm ML-DSA from FIPS 204.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns one object identifier per parameter set (ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87) with absent parameters, puts the raw FIPS 204 public key in SubjectPublicKeyInfo, restricts key usage to signing, and defines seed, expanded and both formats for private keys.
tldr.outcome: ML-DSA certificates can be issued and validated in a uniform way. The pre-hash variant HashML-DSA is forbidden in PKIX, with the External mu mode described as the alternative.

today: RFC 9881 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the X.509 profile in RFC 5280.

sections.title: ML-DSA in Certificates
sections.content:
The Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) is a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme standardized by NIST in FIPS 204. This document specifies its use in Internet X.509 (PKIX) certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) at three security levels: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87.

FIPS 204 defines a pure and a pre-hash variant of ML-DSA. Only the pure variant is specified here; the reasoning is in the operational considerations. Before standardization ML-DSA was known as Dilithium, and the two are not compatible.

The base certificate and CRL formats come from RFC 5280. This RFC only adds what is specific to ML-DSA: identifiers, encodings and rules for keys and signatures.
sections.eli5: Certificates are like digital ID cards, and each one carries a signature. This document says how to sign them with a brand-new kind of signature that is meant to stay safe in the future.

sections.title: Identifiers and Parameter Sets
sections.content:
Each parameter set has its own NIST-registered object identifier (OID): id-ml-dsa-44, id-ml-dsa-65 and id-ml-dsa-87. They sit under the NIST signature algorithms arc and end in 17, 18 and 19 respectively. The OID goes in the algorithm field of an AlgorithmIdentifier, and the parameters component MUST be absent.

The three sets target NIST post-quantum security categories 2, 3 and 5. An appendix explains that NIST defines levels against reference schemes: level 3 and level 5 use AES-192 and AES-256 key search, while levels 2 and 4 use collision search for SHA-256 and SHA-384. The sizes below are raw keys and signatures, without ASN.1 wrapper overhead.
sections.eli5: There are three sizes of the lock, small, medium and large. Each one gets its own name tag, and the bigger ones are harder to break but take more room.

sections.title: Signatures on Certificates and CRLs
sections.content:
In a certificate, the signature is carried in signatureAlgorithm and signatureValue, and in a CRL the same way. The identifiers from the previous section are used both there and in the signature field of TBSCertificate and TBSCertList. The AlgorithmIdentifier SHALL be a SEQUENCE of one component, the OID.

The signature is computed over the ASN.1 DER-encoded TBSCertificate or TBSCertList. The optional context string ctx from FIPS 204 is left at its default, the empty string.

Conforming CAs MUST specify the algorithm explicitly using these OIDs. Conforming clients that process ML-DSA certificates and CRLs MUST recognize the OIDs. ASN.1 classes sa-ml-dsa-44, sa-ml-dsa-65 and sa-ml-dsa-87 tie each OID to its public key type (the definitions come from RFC 5912).
sections.eli5: The authority stamps the certificate with its signature and writes the name of the stamp type on it. Anyone checking must know all three stamp names.

sections.title: Public Keys and Key Usage
sections.content:
In the certificate's subjectPublicKeyInfo, the algorithm holds the OID and the subjectPublicKey BIT STRING holds the raw byte-string encoding from FIPS 204 (Algorithm 22), with no further ASN.1 wrapping. Outside that structure the key may be an OCTET STRING of exactly 1312 bytes (ML-DSA-44), 1952 bytes (ML-DSA-65) or 2592 bytes (ML-DSA-87).

If a keyUsage extension is present, it MUST have at least one of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign or cRLSign set. It MUST NOT have keyEncipherment, dataEncipherment, keyAgreement, encipherOnly or decipherOnly set, because ML-DSA keys cannot establish keys or encrypt data.
sections.eli5: The public key is the part everyone may see, so it goes right on the card. This key can only prove who signed something. It cannot lock secret messages.

sections.title: Private Key Formats
sections.content:
FIPS 204 has two private key forms: a 32-octet seed and an expanded private key computed from it with ML-DSA.KeyGen_internal. Inside a OneAsymmetricKey (RFC 5958), the private key is a CHOICE of three DER-encoded forms: seed (tag [0], a 32-byte OCTET STRING), expandedKey (an OCTET STRING of 2560, 4032 or 4896 bytes by level) and both (a SEQUENCE holding the two).

The seed format is RECOMMENDED because it is the most compact and lets both the expanded and public keys be derived. The RFC points out that expanding a seed is one-way, so once the seed is discarded it cannot be recreated from the expanded key. It therefore RECOMMENDS that implementations retain and export the seed even when also exporting the expanded key. Parsers should tell the forms apart by their ASN.1 tags (0x80, 0x04 and 0x30), not by length.

When a recipient gets a key with both seed and expanded key, it SHOULD run a consistency check by regenerating the expanded form from the seed and comparing bytes. If the check is done and fails, the recipient MUST reject the key as malformed.
sections.eli5: The seed is a tiny recipe card and the expanded key is the whole finished cake. You can bake the cake from the card, but you can never get the card back from the cake, so keep the card.

sections.title: Why HashML-DSA Is Not Allowed
sections.content:
The HashML-DSA mode from FIPS 204 MUST NOT be used in X.509 certificates for CRLs, OCSP, certificate issuance and related PKIX protocols. The main reason is interoperability. ML-DSA and HashML-DSA are incompatible and need different verify routines, and since the same OIDs identify the public keys and signature algorithms, a key would have to be committed to one type when the certificate is created. That is hard to know in advance for operators.

There is also a small security argument. ML-DSA prepends a SHAKE256 hash of the public key to the message before hashing, so a collision against the hash alone would not be enough for an attack. HashML-DSA loses that property, but the RFC calls the practical risk in X.509 immaterial, since the issuer's key hash is already in the signed Authority Key Identifier extension.

Applications that need pre-hashing can use the External mu mode instead. An appendix gives modified algorithms for it (Computeμ and Signμ).
sections.eli5: There are two ways to sign, and they cannot read each other's signatures. To avoid mix-ups, this document allows only the plain way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 apply. ML-DSA is strongly unforgeable under chosen message attacks, and strength estimates assume the attacker sees signatures for no more than 2^{64} chosen messages.

ML-DSA depends on high-quality random numbers, and a weak generator for key generation might let an attacker recover the private key by trying a small set of possibilities. The design avoids Gaussian sampling to ease side-channel resilience, but implementers must still take great care. Some leakage has been shown in the bit-unpacking part of signing, and masking countermeasures exist at a performance cost.

Signing can be deterministic or randomized, and a verifier cannot tell the two apart. Deterministic signing is easier to test and needs no randomness source. Randomized signing mixes in a 256-bit random string and is easier to harden against fault and side-channel attacks. The RFC also notes that ML-DSA has the non-repudiation-related properties of exclusive ownership, message-bound signatures and non-resignability.
sections.eli5: A good lock needs a truly random key, and you still have to hide it from people who might spy on how you turn it.
